5.5 Alternative Assets

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

Investments other than stocks, bonds and cash are called alternative assets. They are often promoted as a way to diversify and raise returns. This lesson looks at each in turn: where its return comes from, what its risks are, and why its published figures need careful reading.

Real estate investment trusts

Section titled “Real estate investment trusts”

A real estate investment trust (REIT) is a company that owns and runs real estate such as offices, apartments, warehouses and data centers. Under US tax law, a REIT must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income as dividends and hold at least 75% of its assets in real estate; if it meets these conditions, it pays essentially no income tax at the company level, and its income passes straight to shareholders.

Listed REITs trade on exchanges every day like stocks, so investors can hold a diversified real estate portfolio with little money, without buying buildings themselves. A REIT’s return comes from rents (dividends) and changes in property values; REITs usually borrow a lot (financial leverage), and when rates rise, their borrowing costs rise and property valuations fall (3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models). Since most profits must be paid out, REITs grow mainly by issuing new shares and borrowing.

Check C1
REITs own physical buildings and their income is mainly steady rent, so adding listed REITs to a stock portfolio diversifies about as well as adding bonds.
Where are listed REITs priced, and by whom? Do their leverage and their sensitivity to the economy and to rates make them more like bonds or more like stocks?

Commodities

Section titled “Commodities”

Commodities such as oil, metals and farm products produce no cash flows: a barrel of oil pays no dividend, and storing it costs money. So investors usually do not hold the physical goods but gain exposure to commodity prices through futures (futures contract). Holding futures and rolling into the next contract before expiry, the total return can be split into three parts:

R=ΔS+y+rcR = \Delta S + y + r_cR=ΔS+y+rc​

ΔS\Delta SΔS is the change in the spot price, yyy is the roll yield (positive when the later contract is cheaper than the expiring one, negative in contango (contango)), and rcr_crc​ is the interest earned on the cash held as margin. A commodity fund’s return can therefore differ greatly from the spot price changes in the news (5.1 Forwards and Futures).

The long-run return of commodities is disputed: Gorton and Rouwenhorst (2006), using data for 1959–2004, found that a diversified portfolio of commodity futures earned returns similar to stocks; Erb and Harvey (2006) argued that the long-run average return of individual commodities is close to 0, and that portfolio returns came mainly from regular rebalancing and roll yield, which need not repeat.

Check C2
In years when inflation rises unexpectedly, a diversified portfolio of commodity futures tends to do well, while stocks and long-term bonds tend to do poorly.
Inflation measures the prices of what? How does unexpected inflation affect interest rates and the prices of long-term bonds?

Hedge funds

Section titled “Hedge funds”

A hedge fund is an investment fund that raises money only from wealthy investors and institutions, is lightly regulated, and may sell short and use leverage and derivatives; strategies include long–short equity, macro, arbitrage and event-driven investing. Hedge funds charge two kinds of fees: a management fee, a fixed percentage of assets, and an incentive fee, a percentage of returns. The traditional standard is “2 and 20”: a 2% management fee and a 20% incentive fee; average levels have fallen in recent years. The incentive fee usually has a high-water mark: the fund’s value must exceed its previous peak before an incentive fee is charged again.

Hedge fund indexes come from databases to which funds report voluntarily and suffer from survivorship bias and backfill bias (survivorship bias); studies estimate these biases at up to several percentage points a year. Moreover, many strategies earn steady returns in normal times and then lose heavily in crises, as if they had sold puts (5.2 Option Basics).

Check C3
Under the default settings of Figure 3-1, fees take 36% of each year's return but 57% of the total 20-year gain. The main reason is:
In the figure the incentive fee is always 20%, and the management fee does not change. Does the share taken each year change?
A high-water mark can only reduce incentive fees after a loss, and here every year's return is positive. Where does the difference come from?

Private equity and private markets

Section titled “Private equity and private markets”

Private equity funds buy stakes in unlisted companies, or take listed companies private, often with heavy borrowing (leveraged buyouts), and sell them after several years of restructuring. Venture capital is private equity that invests in start-ups. Private credit and private real estate are organized in a similar way.

Such funds usually last about 10 years. Investors first commit an amount; the fund calls it in installments as it finds deals and returns money in installments as it sells them. Early on there are only outflows and management fees and the returns come later, so the cumulative cash flow first falls and then rises, which is called the J-curve. Investors can hardly exit during the fund’s life; this illiquidity premium is one of the main reasons private investments should offer higher returns.

The performance of private funds is often stated with two measures: the internal rate of return (internal rate of return), and the ratio of the total amount returned to the amount invested (the multiple). The two can rank funds differently (Exercises Question 2). Private assets have no daily market prices; each quarter the fund reports values based on appraisals or the manager’s own models.

Check C4
A private real estate fund's reported quarterly returns have an annualized volatility of only 6% and a correlation of only 0.2 with stocks, giving a Sharpe ratio far above that of stocks. The most reasonable explanation is:
Are an office building's tenants, rents and financing costs shielded from a recession just because there is no daily quote? Does the lack of a quote change the risk itself, or the numbers we see?
Skill could explain a higher average return, but can it explain why both the volatility and the correlation with stocks are so low?

Crypto assets

Section titled “Crypto assets”

A crypto asset is a digital asset recorded on a blockchain. Bitcoin was launched in 2009, with a cap of 21 million coins. In January 2024 the US Securities and Exchange Commission approved spot bitcoin ETFs, so individuals can buy it as they would a stock.

Crypto assets are very volatile: bitcoin’s annualized volatility is often between 50% and 80%, 3 to 5 times that of stocks; it has several times fallen more than 70% from a peak, for example by more than 80% from December 2017 to December 2018 and by about 77% from November 2021 to November 2022. Many other tokens fell to nearly 0. In November 2022 the exchange FTX collapsed after misusing customer funds; customers’ money was frozen and could be recovered only through bankruptcy proceedings.

Check C5
Why can bitcoin not be given an intrinsic value by discounting cash flows, the way 3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models and 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow value stocks?
Many start-up stocks are also very volatile and can still be valued from expected cash flows, just with great uncertainty. Is it the discount rate bitcoin lacks, or something else?
What is one bitcoin a claim on? Will its holder ever share in anyone's profits?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Listed REITs are companies that own real estate; they must distribute most of their income, use high leverage and trade on exchanges every day.
  • A commodity futures return = change in the spot price + roll yield + interest on margin; the long-run return is disputed.
  • Hedge funds charge management and incentive fees; their indexes suffer from survivorship and backfill bias.
  • Private equity is illiquid and valued by appraisal; IRR and the multiple can rank funds differently.
  • Crypto assets have very large swings and drawdowns, and trading platforms themselves can fail.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A hedge fund charges a 2% management fee (at the end of each year, on the value before fees) and a 20% incentive fee (after the management fee, only on the part above the high-water mark, which starts at 100). An investor puts in 100, and the fund's returns before fees in three years are +20%, −20% and +20%.
(a) What is the investor's value after three years? What percentage of the total gain before fees is taken by fees?
(b) The fund's marketing says: "We charge an incentive fee only when we make money for you, so our interests are fully aligned with yours." Evaluate this statement. From the manager's point of view, what kind of option is the incentive fee like? What incentive does the manager have when the fund's value is far below the high-water mark?
Question 2
Two private equity funds each call 100 from investors in the same year. Fund A returns 160 in one payment at the end of year 2; fund B returns 250 in one payment at the end of year 8. Ignore fees and any other cash flows.
(a) What are the IRR and the multiple of each fund?
(b) Fund A's marketing says: "Our IRR is more than twice B's; our performance is far ahead." Evaluate this statement. If the 160 received from A can only be invested in a listed stock index fund with an expected return of 8%, what is the wealth under each choice at the end of year 8? When is A really better?
Question 3
A private real estate fund's appraisal-based annual returns have an average excess return of 4.8% and a volatility of 8%. A simple model says the reported return is a weighted average of the true return and last period's reported return: rt∗=(1−a) rt+a rt−1∗r^*_t = (1 - a)\,r_t + a\,r^*_{t-1}rt∗​=(1−a)rt​+art−1∗​, in which case the reported volatility equals the true volatility times 1−a1+a\sqrt{\frac{1 - a}{1 + a}}1+a1−a​​. For such funds, aaa is about 0.6.
(a) What is the Sharpe ratio on the reported figures? By this model, what are the true volatility and Sharpe ratio, roughly?
(b) A consultant puts the reported figures into a mean–variance optimizer and concludes the portfolio should hold 40% in such funds, "because its Sharpe ratio is twice that of stocks and its correlation with stocks is low". Evaluate this advice.
Question 4
An investor holds 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Stocks have a volatility of 16%, bonds 6%, and their correlation is 0. He plans to switch 5% of the portfolio into bitcoin (cutting stocks and bonds in proportion to 57% and 38%); bitcoin has a volatility of 70%, a correlation of 0.4 with stocks and 0 with bonds.
(a) What is the portfolio's volatility before and after adding bitcoin? After adding it, what percentage of the portfolio variance comes from bitcoin? (Asset iii's contribution to portfolio variance is wiCov⁡(Ri,Rp)w_i \operatorname{Cov}(R_i, R_p)wi​Cov(Ri​,Rp​).)
(b) He says: "It's only 5%; even if bitcoin goes to zero I lose only 5%, so the effect on the risk of the whole portfolio is small." Evaluate this statement.
